A `Stream<T>` delivers a sequence of async events over time. Like an async iterator.

### Single-subscription (default)
- Only ONE listener at a time
- Can pause/resume the producer
- **Use for**: file reading, HTTP body, socket

### Broadcast
- MULTIPLE simultaneous listeners
- Cannot pause producer
- **Use for**: user input events, pub/sub, `ChangeNotifier`-style

`StreamController` — creates and exposes a stream you can push events into.
`async*` generator — simplest way to create streams with `yield`.

`StreamController` gives you a stream plus a sink you push events into, so any callback-based source can become a Stream.

### Built into dart:async
- `map()` — transform each event
- `where()` — filter events
- `take(n)` / `skip(n)` — limit or skip events
- `distinct()` — drop consecutive duplicates
- `asyncMap()` — map through an async function, one event at a time
- `expand()` — turn one event into many
- `transform()` — plug in a `StreamTransformer` of your own

### Only in rxdart
- `debounceTime()` — emit after a period of silence; the search-box operator
- `throttleTime()` — emit at most once per window
- `switchMap()` — cancel the previous inner stream when a new event arrives
- `scan()` — running accumulator, like `fold` but streaming
- `startWith()` / `combineLatest` / `withLatestFrom`

For a search box the chain is `debounceTime`, then `distinct`, then `switchMap` — so the in-flight request for "flu" is cancelled the moment "flut" arrives.

A call to `listen` hands back a StreamSubscription — your only handle to pause, resume or cancel delivery. Ignore the return value and you can never stop listening.

### Methods
- `cancel()` — stop receiving events; for single-subscription streams, frees the producer too
- `pause([Future resumeSignal])` — pause delivery; events buffer or backpressure depending on the source
- `resume()` — resume delivery
- `onData / onError / onDone` — replace the handlers post-construction

### Lifecycle rules
- If the State that owns the subscription is unmounted, the subscription must be cancelled in dispose() — otherwise the callback fires on a dead state and crashes (or, worse, leaks objects via a closure over `this`)
- `cancel()` is idempotent and returns Future\<void> — wait for it if you need to be sure cleanup ran
- On a single-subscription stream, cancel propagates to the producer (e.g. async\* generator stops at its current yield, file handle closes)
- On a broadcast stream, your cancel only removes you — other subscribers and the producer continue

A common bug: using `stream.listen(onData)` and forgetting the return value — you can't cancel later. Always assign to a field if the subscription needs to outlive the listen call.

Two ways to consume a stream — both delegate to the same subscription mechanism, but they shape your code very differently.

`await for (final x in stream) { ... }`:
- **Sequential** — the loop body MUST complete before the next event is delivered
- **Backpressure** — if your loop body is slow, the producer is paused (single-subscription) or events buffer (broadcast)
- Easy to read; reads like a for-loop
- Cannot easily attach error handlers other than try/catch around the loop
- Use when the consumer needs to do bounded work per event in order

`stream.listen(onData)`:
- **Reactive** — onData fires per event; your `listen` returns immediately
- Events arrive even if the previous handler hasn't finished — you handle concurrency yourself
- Lets you pass `onError`, `onDone`, `cancelOnError`
- Must keep the subscription handle for cancel/pause
- Use when you want fine-grained control or async handlers that should run concurrently

### Gotchas
- `await for` on a broadcast stream is fine but you can't easily share that loop with another consumer — listen is more flexible for fan-out
- `await for` cannot be cancelled from outside — break out of the loop on a sentinel event
- Inside an async\* function, `await for` paired with `yield` lets you transform a stream cleanly

Errors on a stream are first-class events delivered through the error channel — they don't throw at the listen call site. The handler chain offers several places to react.

### Where errors land
- `stream.listen(onData, onError: ...)` — handler receives (Object error, StackTrace stack)
- `stream.handleError((e, s) {...})` — pipeline operator that catches and either swallows or rethrows
- `await for` — wrap in try/catch; if cancelOnError is true (default), the iteration stops on first error
- `transformer` — convert errors into typed events (e.g. wrap into `Result.err`)

### Cancel-on-error
- Default for `await for` and `Stream.first`
- Default for `stream.listen` is `cancelOnError: false` — loop continues; pass true if you want it to stop on first error

### Design tips
- For a Bloc/Riverpod pipeline, transform errors INTO state. Don't let the stream simply close on a transient network blip — emit `Failed(e)` and let the next user action retry.
- Use `handleError` to scope which errors the rest of the pipeline sees. Common pattern: `handleError((e) { if (e is FormatException) ...; else throw e; })`
- Don't `print` — emit to your logger and decide whether to rethrow

Gotcha: a thrown synchronous error inside an async\* function becomes an error event on the resulting stream. If your generator throws inside a loop, surrounding code that does `listen(onError: ...)` catches it; surrounding code that does `await for` catches it via try/catch.

rxdart wraps dart:async with the Rx-style operators that are standard in other reactive libraries (RxJava, RxJS). The core stream model is the same — rxdart's classes are still Streams — but it gives you operators that are tedious to hand-roll.

### BehaviorSubject\<T>
- Like a broadcast StreamController that always replays the LAST value to a new listener
- **Useful for state-like streams**: a UI that subscribes mid-flow still sees the current value
- Combined with `.value` getter for synchronous reads

### ReplaySubject\<T>
- Replays the last N (or all) values to new listeners
- Useful for event logs and stateful caches

### Key operators not in dart:async
- `debounceTime` — emit only after a period of silence (great for search input)
- `throttleTime` — emit at most once per period
- `switchMap` — when a new event arrives, cancel the in-flight inner stream from the previous event (search-as-you-type cancellation pattern)
- `combineLatest` / `combineLatest2`...— combine the latest values from multiple streams into one
- `startWith(value)` — prepend an initial value
- `withLatestFrom` — pair each event with the latest from another stream
- `bufferTime` / `windowTime` — group events by time window

### When NOT to add rxdart
- You're using Riverpod and most operators have equivalents in providers + Notifiers — extra dependency may not be worth it
- **Single-screen, tiny pipeline** — handcraft the missing operator with async\*

Gotcha: BehaviorSubject is broadcast — multiple listeners share the same subscription. Closing the subject is on you.

Three combinators cover most multi-stream patterns. Same names show up in RxDart, RxJS, and dart:async helpers.

### merge
- Forward EVERY event from EVERY input stream, in arrival order
- **Use when**: "show any error from any source" / "collect events from multiple chats"
- `Rx.merge([a, b, c])` (rxdart), or `StreamGroup.merge` (dart:async)

### zip
- Pair the i-th event of each input. Output is `[a₀, b₀, c₀]`, then `[a₁, b₁, c₁]`, ...
- If one input runs out, output stops — slowest input is the bottleneck
- **Use when**: "render output i = f(streamA\[i], streamB\[i])"
- `Rx.zip2(a, b, (x, y) => ...)` etc.

### combineLatest
- Whenever ANY input emits, emit a tuple of the LATEST value from each input
- Output starts only when EVERY input has emitted at least once
- **Use when**: "derived state — recompute when any input changes"
- `Rx.combineLatest2/3/...`

### Other useful combinators (rxdart)
- `concat([a, b, c])` — drain a, then b, then c (sequential)
- `withLatestFrom(other)` — emit when source emits, paired with other's latest
- `startWith(value)` — prepend a seed value

For Riverpod users: most of this can be expressed with derived providers (each `ref.watch` is a combineLatest under the hood). For BLoC, rxdart's combinators are the standard tool.

Backpressure is what happens when a producer emits faster than its consumer can process. Streams answer that very differently depending on their type and how you consume them.

### Single-subscription stream
- Producer is paused when the consumer pauses or is slow inside `await for`
- `pause(Future)` on the subscription tells the producer to stop until the future completes
- **Built-in backpressure** — pausing the subscription makes events buffer instead of firing; nothing about `add(...)` itself blocks, it's an `async*` generator's `yield` that actually suspends the producer until the consumer is ready
- Examples that respect this naturally: HTTP body streams, file IO, async generators that `await` between yields

### Broadcast stream
- **NO backpressure** — the producer doesn't know about specific listeners and can't pause itself
- Each listener sees every event when it's emitted; if the listener can't keep up, events queue inside the engine and memory grows
- Use this for fast, small events (UI events, pubsub messages) — never for high-volume data streams

### When you have a fast producer and slow consumer
- Convert the source to a single-subscription stream (don't use broadcast just for convenience)
- **Buffer or window** — `bufferTime`, `bufferCount` — collapse N events into one batch your consumer can process
- **Sample / throttle** — drop intermediate events you can ignore (cursor positions, sensor data)
- Sink-based push with a bounded queue — apply your own quota and drop or coalesce when full

Common mistake: using a `StreamController.broadcast()` for an event log that fans out to dozens of subscribers, while one subscriber writes to disk synchronously. Memory grows during disk slow-downs because broadcast has no backpressure. The fix is either (a) a faster consumer, (b) a per-listener bounded queue, or (c) a different fan-out mechanism (a database with notifications).

Future = ONE event at SOME point. Stream = ZERO-or-more events over time. The choice shapes everything from your error handling to your testing.

### Return a Future when
- The operation has a single result — fetch a user, post a form, read a file
- The caller wants to compose with `await`
- Errors are exceptional (a thrown error stops the awaited expression)

### Return a Stream when
- The operation produces multiple values over time — websocket messages, sensor readings, paginated results yielded as you fetch them
- The caller wants to react incrementally — partial UI rendering, progress indicators
- **Backpressure or pause/resume matters** — file streaming, video frames

### Paginated APIs are a great test
- Fetch one page → return Future\<Page\<T>> (caller calls again for the next page; explicit)
- Iterate ALL items → return Stream\<T> (consumer can `await for` and stop when satisfied; built-in backpressure)
- Both can be useful in the same codebase; choose by the consumer's needs

When in doubt, prefer Future. Streams are more powerful but more complex — you commit your callers to subscription management. Streams that emit exactly one event are usually a sign you should have returned a Future.

### Mixing the two
- Future.asStream() — promote a Future into a single-event stream (rarely needed)
- Stream.first / Stream.last — convert a stream's first/last event into a Future
- Stream.toList() — drain the whole stream into a Future\<List\<T>> (only when you know it's bounded)

StreamBuilder subscribes to the stream, rebuilds on every event, and cancels the subscription when it leaves the tree.

### Everything you get arrives in an AsyncSnapshot
- `connectionState` — none when there is no stream at all, waiting before the first event, active once events are flowing, done when the stream has closed
- `hasData` and `data` — the LATEST event, which the snapshot keeps until the next one
- `hasError` and `error` — the latest error
- `initialData` fills the first frame so the UI does not flash a spinner

### The details that catch people
- `AsyncSnapshot` never carries both at once — an error event resets `data` to null, so a transient error blanks the UI instead of preserving the last good value; hold onto it yourself if you want it to survive an error
- `done` means the stream closed, not that loading succeeded — a closed empty stream never had data
- Building the stream inline in the `stream:` argument re-subscribes on every rebuild. On a single-subscription stream that throws, and on a broadcast one you silently drop events and leak subscriptions. Store the stream in a field or get it from a provider.
- A broadcast stream delivers only what happens after you subscribe, so a StreamBuilder mounted later starts empty. Seed it with initialData, or use a stream that replays its current value such as a BehaviorSubject.
- Everything the builder returns is rebuilt on every event, so keep the subtree small and put the expensive parts outside it

For anything past a single screen-level stream, a BlocBuilder, a StreamProvider or a Riverpod provider gives you the same subscription handling plus caching and testability.

A StreamController turns any push-based callback into a Stream, and its onListen and onCancel hooks are where the underlying resource starts and stops.

### The shape that behaves correctly
- Create the controller as a private field and expose only `controller.stream`, never the sink
- Start the native listener in `onListen`, which means nothing is running until someone actually subscribes
- Tear it down in `onCancel`, so the sensor stops the moment the last listener goes away
- Push with `add`, report failures with `addError` rather than throwing, and `close()` when the source is finished for good
- Guard with `isClosed` before adding, because adding to a closed controller throws a StateError

### Single-subscription or broadcast
- The default single-subscription controller supports pause and resume, so a slow consumer applies real backpressure. Use it for one owner, such as a repository.
- `StreamController.broadcast()` when several widgets subscribe at once. It cannot be paused, and it drops events emitted while nobody is listening.
- With a broadcast controller, onListen fires for the first listener and onCancel when the last one leaves, so the resource can be started and stopped more than once

When the source is itself asynchronous rather than callback-driven, an `async*` generator is simpler — and a `try/finally` around its loop runs when the subscription is cancelled, which is where you release resources.

A controller is also the easiest way to test a stream consumer: hand the widget the controller's stream and push exactly the events, errors and completion your test needs.

A single-subscription stream accepts exactly one listener for its whole life, and cancelling that listener does not free the slot.

What counts as listening is wider than people expect: `listen`, `await for`, `first`, `last`, `toList`, `forEach` and every StreamBuilder each take the one subscription. So the error also appears with a single consumer whose widget rebuilt and subscribed a second time.

Where single-subscription streams come from: a plain `StreamController()`, an `async*` generator, file and socket reads, and HTTP response bodies.

### How to fix it, in the order I would try
- Subscribe once and feed a store. One listener updates a ValueNotifier, a Bloc or a provider, and every widget watches that. Late widgets then see the current value, which a raw stream cannot give them.
- `StreamController.broadcast()` when you own the controller and genuinely need several independent listeners
- `stream.asBroadcastStream()` to adapt a stream you do not own — with the caveat that it starts consuming the source at the first listener, cannot be paused, and gives later subscribers nothing that already happened
- A BehaviorSubject from rxdart when late subscribers must receive the latest value on subscribe

Broadcast is not a free upgrade: events emitted while nobody listens are dropped, there is no backpressure, and every listener must be cancelled individually. If the stream represents state rather than events, the store approach is almost always the better answer.

The `builder` is a pure render function that Flutter may call at any time and any number of times, so anything with a side effect belongs on a subscription instead.

### Why it fires more than once
- The builder runs on every rebuild, not only on stream events — a parent rebuild, a theme or MediaQuery change, a route animation frame and a hot reload all re-run it with the same snapshot
- `AsyncSnapshot` keeps the *latest* event, so a "signed in" value stays in the snapshot for as long as the stream is open; every one of those rebuilds sees it again
- Calling `showSnackBar` or `Navigator.push` during build also throws "setState() or markNeedsBuild() called during build", which is why people reach for `addPostFrameCallback` — and that fires exactly as often

### Where the side effect goes
- Subscribe once in `initState` and do navigation, snackbars and analytics in `onData`; the StreamBuilder keeps doing nothing but rendering
- In bloc that channel is `BlocListener` (`BlocConsumer` when you need both); in Riverpod it is `ref.listen`
- If the stream replays — a BehaviorSubject, a cached last value — make the event consumable: emit a one-shot command, or remember the id you last handled
- Guard the callback with `mounted`, because an event can land between the last frame and `dispose`

The rule of thumb: the builder answers "what does this state look like", the listener answers "what should happen now that this happened". Anything you would be unhappy to run twice is not a rendering concern.

Silence is not an event, so nothing in the pipeline can notice it — you turn the absence of events into an event with `stream.timeout`.

### What timeout actually does
- `stream.timeout(duration)` emits a `TimeoutException` as an error event when no event arrives within that window; the countdown starts when you listen and resets on every event
- Pass `onTimeout: (EventSink<T> sink) { ... }` to decide what happens instead — add a substitute event, add your own typed error, or `sink.close()` to end the stream
- It does not touch the source. The socket subscription stays live, a late event still flows through, and the timeout fires again after another quiet window. Timing out is a signal, not a teardown — cancel the source yourself if you want the connection dropped.

### Making it survive a real network
- A dead TCP connection on mobile can stay open silently for minutes, so liveness has to be active: `IOWebSocketChannel.connect(uri, pingInterval: Duration(seconds: 20))` drives protocol pings on mobile and desktop; there is no `pingInterval` on web, so send your own ping frame and require a reply
- Reconnecting means a *new* stream — a closed channel never reopens. Keep the UI subscribed to a stream you own (a broadcast controller, a Bloc, a Notifier) and swap the socket underneath it with exponential backoff plus jitter.
- Render "stale" as a state, not as the last good value with no marker; a spinner or a price that can be wrong forever is the bug the user actually reports

Rule of thumb: every stream that crosses the network needs a deadline, a heartbeat and a way back.

`distinct` compares each event with the previously emitted one using `==`, and a freshly decoded list of freshly constructed models is never `==` to the last batch.

### What distinct does and does not do
- It remembers the previous *emitted* event and skips an event equal to it; the comparison is `==` unless you pass an `equals` callback
- That memory is per subscription, so on a broadcast stream every listener filters independently — and a late subscriber has no previous value, so its first event always gets through
- Dart's default `==` is identity, for your model classes and for `List` alike, so two structurally identical payloads are simply two different objects

### Making the comparison real
- Give the model value equality: override `==`/`hashCode` with `Object.hash`, use a record, or generate it with Equatable or freezed
- For collections, `==` on `List` is still identity — compare element-wise with `ListEquality` from package:collection, or skip the whole problem by comparing a version: `distinct((a, b) => a.etag == b.etag)` beats deep-comparing a thousand rows every second
- Narrow before you compare: `map` to exactly the slice the widget draws and then `distinct`, so a badge that shows a count watches an `int` rather than a list

Then scope the rebuild. Even a correct `distinct` leaves one StreamBuilder wrapped around the whole page — wrap only the subtree that actually changes, and hoist the constant parts out of the builder so they are not rebuilt along with it.

A Stream has no current value: `first` subscribes, waits for the next event *after* that moment, then cancels — so on a stream that has already emitted, you are waiting for the one after.

### What first actually does
- It listens, takes the first event to arrive after the listen, cancels the subscription and completes the future
- On a broadcast stream everything emitted before that instant is gone, including the value the UI is showing right now
- If the stream closes without emitting, `first` throws `StateError: No element`; `firstWhere` does the same unless you pass `orElse`
- On a single-subscription stream it burns the one allowed subscription, so the next `listen` fails with "Stream has already been listened to"
- Nothing bounds the wait, so a quiet source hangs the caller forever unless you add `.timeout`

### Give the value a home
- Keep the latest value somewhere it can be read synchronously: a field in the repository, a `ValueNotifier`, a rxdart `BehaviorSubject` with `.value`, or Bloc/Riverpod state
- Design the API as a pair — `Future<T> current()` for "what is it now" and `Stream<T> changes()` for "tell me when it moves" — instead of making callers mine a stream for state
- When one event really is what you want, bound it: `await feed.quotes.first.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5))`

Mental model: a stream is a sequence of things that happen, not a variable you can read. If you need a variable, keep a variable.

No — asynchronous delivery is the contract, not a bug, and `sync: true` "fixes" the symptom by handing arbitrary listener code control in the middle of your own `add` call.

### Why add is asynchronous
- `add` schedules delivery; the listener runs in a later microtask, so the statements after `add` always finish first
- That guarantee is what lets you `add` before anyone has listened — a single-subscription controller buffers — and what keeps an exception thrown by a listener from surfacing inside the producer
- It also fixes ordering: every listener sees events in emission order regardless of what any of them does when it runs

### What sync: true actually changes
- The listener is invoked on the `add` call stack, but only when a subscription exists and is not paused; otherwise the event is buffered as usual. "Sometimes synchronous" is the worst kind of contract.
- Re-entrancy: the listener can `add` again, dispatch a bloc event or call `setState` while the producer is halfway through updating its own state
- An exception from the listener now propagates out of `add`, into a producer that has no idea what to do with it
- dart:async limits it to one case: a controller whose `add` is already driven by another asynchronous event, purely to skip an extra microtask hop

### The fix in tests
- Let the queue turn: `await pumpEventQueue()` from package:test, or `await Future<void>.delayed(Duration.zero)`
- Better, assert on the stream itself with `expectLater` and the stream matchers, so timing stops being your problem
- Use `fakeAsync` when timers are in play, so debounce and timeout windows are deterministic

`close()` returns the controller's `done` future, and on a single-subscription controller that future completes only once a listener has received the done event — with no listener, the buffered events and the done event just sit there.

### The rule behind it
- A non-broadcast controller buffers everything you add until someone listens, precisely so nothing is lost; `done` is the promise that a consumer saw the end, not an acknowledgement that you called `close`
- A subscription that cancels also completes `done` — cancelling is a legitimate end of the conversation
- `StreamController.broadcast()` behaves differently: it never buffers, so `close()` completes on the next turn whether or not anyone is listening
- `done` is also where an error the consumer never handled shows up, so `await close()` can throw as well as hang

### How to close safely
- Do not `await close()` on a path that must finish. `dispose()` is synchronous anyway, so `unawaited(_controller.close())` from dart:async is the honest expression of "stop, I am not waiting".
- If you want the awaited version, make the controller broadcast or guarantee a subscriber for its whole life
- `addStream(source)` returns its own future and locks the controller while it runs: `add`, `addError` and `close` all throw "Bad state: Cannot add event while adding a stream" until it completes, so await it first
- Guard producers with `isClosed`, because adding after close throws a StateError that usually nobody catches

Mental model: `close()` is a message to the consumer, not a kill switch. With no consumer there is nobody to answer it.

An error event with no `onError` handler on the subscription is neither swallowed nor thrown at the `add` site — it goes to `Zone.current.handleUncaughtError` for the zone in which `listen` was called.

### How the error gets out
- `stream.listen(onData)` with no `onError` is the whole bug: data has a handler, errors do not, so every error escapes the pipeline
- `forEach`, `toList` and `pipe` push the error into the future they return instead, and an unawaited future error is an uncaught error too
- In Flutter that zone handler is `PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError` (or your `runZonedGuarded` wrapper around `runApp`). `FlutterError.onError` never sees it — that channel carries framework errors from build, layout and gesture callbacks.
- A broadcast controller with no listener at that moment drops the error silently; a single-subscription one buffers it and detonates when someone finally listens

### Handling it where it belongs
- Give every `listen` an `onError`, or terminate the pipeline with `handleError` at the boundary between the data layer and the UI
- `cancelOnError` defaults to `false` for `listen` but `true` for `await for`, `first` and `forEach`, so one blip silently ends an `await for` loop and the stream merely looks quiet afterwards
- Convert transport failures into state — `Degraded(e)` — so the UI has something to render and a retry to offer, instead of an error event nobody consumes
- Keep the top-level handlers installed anyway: they are the net that tells you which stream you forgot, and they carry the stack trace from the original `addError`

Rule: an error event is handled only where someone subscribed with a handler. Everywhere else it is a crash report with your name on it.

Wrap it in a `StreamQueue` from package:async: it takes the one subscription for you and turns the stream into a pull API you can read a piece at a time, then gives the remainder back as a stream.

### The pull API
- `next` completes with the next event and throws `StateError` if the stream ended first; `peek` reads it without consuming; `hasNext` tells you whether one is coming
- `take(n)`, `skip(n)` and `lookAhead(n)` do the same in bulk
- `rest` returns the remaining events as a stream and transfers ownership — after that the queue is spent and its other methods throw
- `cancel()` releases the source subscription, `cancel(immediate: true)` without waiting for pending requests. Always cancel on the failure path, or you leak the subscription and whatever it holds open.

### Why this beats hand-rolling it
- The queue holds the single subscription for the whole conversation, so "Stream has already been listened to" cannot happen between the header read and the parser
- It pauses the source while no request is outstanding, so a slow parser applies real backpressure to the socket instead of buffering inside your code
- `startTransaction()` and `withTransaction` let you look ahead and rewind: read enough to decide which protocol version this is, then hand all of it, unconsumed, to the right parser
- It works on any single-subscription stream — sockets, `File.openRead()`, an `async*` generator, `stdin`

Mental model: `listen` is push, and push means handling whatever arrives whenever it arrives. A StreamQueue is pull, which is what protocol code actually wants.
